extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, storytellers, and students/scholars of narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Apply or analyze Christopher Booker’s model of seven (plus two) basic plot archetypes, the five-stage 'meta-plot' progression within each, and the implied quality criteria for crafting or critiquing stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming the Monster
rubrics_metrics.description: Hero confronts a great evil that threatens the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic examples: Beowulf, Star Wars, Jaws. Use when the central conflict is a clear external antagonist/evil force; plot emphasizes confrontation and defeat of that menace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rags to Riches
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cinderella, David Copperfield, Aladdin. Emphasize transformation from lowly status to elevated position; often features fortune, recognition, or social mobility as payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Quest
rubrics_metrics.description: Hero travels to acquire an object/place against obstacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Odyssey, Lord of the Rings, Raiders. Structure centers on journey, successive trials/obstacles, and the goal-object/place. Use episodic challenges to develop character and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage and Return
rubrics_metrics.description: Hero visits a strange world, returns home with experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alice, Robinson Crusoe, The Wizard of Oz. Emphasize transformative experience of the 'other' world and the lesson/experience the protagonist brings back to ordinary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion, light tone, resolution in marriages/reconciliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A Midsummer Night's Dream, Bridget Jones. Expect misdirection, misunderstandings, and a final reconciliation or social restoration rather than tragic loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Flawed hero whose downfall results from character flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macbeth, Anna Karenina. Central criterion is a protagonist flaw leading to downfall; the emotional effect is catharsis through loss and recognition of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebirth
rubrics_metrics.description: Hero falls under shadow then is redeemed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Scrooge, Sleeping Beauty, Beauty and the Beast. Narrative arc moves from corruption/decay to renewal and moral/regenerative awakening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebellion (additional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot driven by resistance against an oppressive force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as a later additional plot type — example: 1984. Use when central conflict is systemic/oppressive power and the narrative centers on defiance or overthrow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mystery (additional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot centered on discovery of a hidden truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Later-added plot type emphasizing investigation, revelation, and the gradual uncovering of concealed facts or motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: The 'Meta-Plot' (stages within each)
rubrics_metrics.description: Five recurring stages within each plot: Anticipation, Dream, Frustration, Nightmare, Resolution/Miraculous Escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage details: Anticipation Stage — hero called to adventure; Dream Stage — initial success and illusion of invincibility; Frustration Stage — obstacles mount and reversals begin; Nightmare Stage — apparent defeat; Resolution/Miraculous Escape — hero overcomes through transformation. Use this sequence to map pacing and emotional trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizable plot pattern
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when subverted, the underlying shape of the plot should be felt by readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booker emphasizes readers' recognition of archetypal shapes; maintain a discernible narrative contour even if you invert or play with expectations. Anti-pattern: a story with no perceptible structural shape that leaves readers unanchored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character matched to plot type
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist's qualities should suit the story's plot shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example guidance: tragic protagonists should plausibly possess the flaw leading to downfall; quest heroes should have motivations that justify journeying. Mismatch between protagonist and plot reduces credibility and emotional payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis appropriate to plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The story's emotional resolution should fit its plot type (e.g., comedy → reconciliation; tragedy → grief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the ending delivers the emotional response readers expect from that archetype. Anti-pattern: delivering a cheerful resolution for a story set up as tragedy, or vice versa, without credible transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories work, Booker argues, when they affirm a moral order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain internal moral logic and consequences that align with the story's values; inconsistency in moral cause/effect undermines the story's persuasiveness and reader satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework limitation / reader-expectation model
rubrics_metrics.description: Booker's framework is influential as a 'reader expectation' model but is criticized as too rigid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the model to anticipate reader responses to archetypal shapes rather than as a prescriptive checklist; be aware scholars note many stories don't fit cleanly into these categories. Treat the plots as descriptive tools, not absolute rules.
